rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop and makes that discipline part of the strategy: “Do not assert the program is unprofitable or a halo — the only fact is the non-disclosure.” B has better breadth, but “Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away” is boardroom fan fiction dressed as analysis. Extra angles do not beat grounded angles.
gaps_in_A: “Patagonia opens free repairs at every US store” overstates the offer unless it immediately says basic repairs are free and complex repairs are charged at cost.
“500,000 resold items is the lead” is fragile without a timeframe, run rate, or economic denominator; A names the hole, but the angle still lives or dies there.
“right to repair” is a tempting adjacency, but no current right-to-repair peg was supplied; pitch it raw and it starts looking borrowed.
A underuses “Patagonia is privately held and directs profits to environmental causes” as a possible ownership/business-model lens.
gaps_in_B: “Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away” is unsupported and sloppy. Privately held does not mean no shareholders, and “only” is an invented universal claim.
“no quarterly earnings call where a margin-eating cost center gets killed” invents drama and economics the update does not provide.
“triages it into free/at-cost/resale” invents a repair-to-resale operational workflow. The facts say repair and resale both exist, not that dropped-off items route into resale.
“The prevailing model in apparel is volume” may be plausible, but it is not in the supplied facts. State it as a reporting question or source it.
